study.title: Proverbs 12 - The practical justice that leads to life
study.overview: This chapter brings together short proverbs about discipline, character, words, work and fidelity. The central contrast is not only between "good" and "más," but between two paths: that of justice, which produces firmness, life and integrity, and that of perversity, which seems to generate immediate advantage, but ends in ruin. The text insists that biblical wisdom appears in concrete attitudes: accepting correction, speaking with truth, working diligently, treating others carefully and living in a way that pleases the Lord.

outline.title: Correction, God's favor and firmness of the righteous
outline.explanation: The first proverbs link love to correction with love of knowledge, and contempt for reproof with foolishness. Then the chapter contrasts the favor of the LORD over the good man with the condemnation of the wicked heart, showing that the final destiny is not defined by appearance, but by relationship with God. Also appears the idea of permanence: the righteous has root that is not ripped off, while the wicked do not remain. The virtuous woman is honor to her husband, but shame erode him inside. The passage concludes with the difference between what God approves and what men despise: true understanding is worth more than empty pride.

outline.title: Humility, work, truth, and words that hurt or heal
outline.explanation: Here the text compares appearance and reality, honor and real needs, showing that it is better to be modest and to have sustenance than to seem important and miss. The righteous even cares for the animals, while even the mercy of the wicked can hide cruelty. Di diligent work is a way to bread, but seeking useless things reveals a lack of judgment. The danger of words also stands out: the sinner is caught by what he speaks, the true comes out of anguish, and speech can be as a sword or as a medicine. Wisdom, therefore, is not just thinking right, but to use the mouth for truth and good.

outline.title: The truth that remains and the path of justice that leads to life
outline.explanation: The third part shows the transience of falsehood and the permanence of truth. There is deception in the heart that plots evil, but joy in those who advise peace. God is pleased with the true lips and reproves the lie. The chapter also deals with prudence, laziness, anxiety and care for others: the foolish heart discloses madness, the diligent governs, anxiety slaughter, and the good word raises. The climax comes in the end: the path of justice is called life, and this path does not lead to death, ending the chapter with the certainty that obedience is the sure way before God.

study.context: The chapter belongs to the sapiential literature of Proverbs, whose typical form is the comparison between two moral paths to teach discernment in daily life. The text does not narrate historical events, but observes the common life: discipline, family, work, speech, relationships and fidelity. Thus, the scenario is that of practical instruction for life before the LORD, in which wisdom is shown by concrete attitudes and not by empty religious discourse.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter states that human life is lived before God, who approves the righteous and reproves the wicked. Correction is an instrument of wisdom, because learning requires humility; rejecting it reveals moral brutality. The text also teaches that character has lasting consequences: justice creates stability, while perversity may seem effective, but does not remain. Words have real moral weight: they can preserve life, seriously hurt or lead to the truth. There is also an ethics of compassion and responsibility: the fair considers even the welfare of animals and acts carefully towards others. Finally, the chapter presents justice not only as an obligation, but as a way of life, contrast to death and the ruin that accompany lies, laziness and evil.

scholarViews.insight: The verse points out that the wicked can prosper for a time, but they do not remain; the family of the righteous remains firm for generations.
The path of religion is presented as a right, safe and pleasant path, in which there is life not only in the end, but also throughout the journey.
A righteous man shows mercy even with animals, and his goodness attains the humblest creation.

questions: How do I react when I am corrected: with humility to learn or with resistance and pride?
Have my words served to heal, promote peace and tell the truth, or to hurt, deceive and feed conflicts?
Does my way of working and caring for responsibilities reveal diligence before God or search for useless shortcuts and things?
study.practice: This week, practice three attitudes of the chapter: receive a correction without defending yourself immediately; speak a true and beneficial word to someone in anxiety; and perform a concrete responsibility with diligence, without laziness or empty appearance. Also examine your way of treating people, including the weakest and most dependent on you, seeking to act with care and compassion. The target of the chapter is not only to know what is right, but to walk in the path of justice.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are selective and do not cover each verse individually; therefore, some applications have been synthesized from the biblical text itself and the commented emphases, without relying on external details. The chapter does not provide specific historical data, and it is not appropriate to infer dates, places or symbols beyond what the text and notes support. The theological reading presented is evangelical and interpretative, not an unanimity statement among commentators.
